failing_part: a single random 70/30 train/test split ... gives a less biased and more precise estimate of performance than bootstrap optimism correction or repeated cross-validation
narrowest_regime: Only when n is so large (many thousands of events) that a 30% hold-out is itself precise and the loss of 30% of training data is negligible, or when a truly external/temporal split is the goal; even then it is not more precise than bootstrap/CV.
reason: The cited Steyerberg et al. 2001 abstract concludes the opposite: split-sample estimates were overly pessimistic with large variability, 10-fold CV had low bias and variability, and bootstrap was best; 'split-sample validation is inefficient, and we recommend bootstrapping'. A split trains on only 70% (pessimistic bias) and evaluates on 30% (high variance), so it is both more biased and less precise at hundreds to a few thousand rows.

citations.cite: Steyerberg EW, Harrell FE Jr, Borsboom GJJM et al. J Clin Epidemiol 2001;54:774-781 (abstract fetched via Europe PMC: split-sample pessimistic and highly variable; bootstrap recommended)

bite_note: Changes the recommended internal-validation method; following it gives a noisier, pessimistic performance estimate and discards 30% of the training data when the sample is a few hundred to a few thousand rows.

failing_part: first delete the rows outside the subgroup and then compute Taylor-linearized variances
narrowest_regime: Deleting is harmless only when every PSU in every stratum contains subgroup members and subgroup sample sizes can be treated as fixed (a post-stratified/fixed-size domain); in general the correct procedure is domain (subpopulation) estimation that keeps all rows with out-of-subgroup contributions zeroed.
reason: The within-PSU subgroup sample size is random under the design, and the linearized variance must include PSUs with no subgroup members (they contribute zero totals). Deleting rows treats subgroup size as fixed, drops those PSUs, can leave single-PSU strata, and understates the SE; the CDC NHANES variance-estimation tutorial says to never delete records and to use the software's subpopulation option. My simulation (6 strata x 2 PSUs, clustered subgroup membership) gave mean SE 0.354 with all rows kept vs 0.310 after deletion against a true SD of 0.436, with 95% CI coverage 0.83 vs 0.76.

citations.cite: CDC/NCHS NHANES tutorial, Variance Estimation: subpopulation analysis, 'never delete or drop records ... use the special statements for subgroup analyses' (fetched; the cited Analytic Guidelines 2011-2016 s3.2.3 PDF itself could not be text-extracted)
West BT, Berglund P, Heeringa SG. A closer examination of subpopulation analysis of complex-sample survey data. Stata J 2008;8:520-531

bite_note: Changes the standard errors and CIs of every survey subgroup estimate (too narrow after deletion) and can break variance estimation with lonely PSUs; the app computing it this way gives anti-conservative inference.

failing_part: any covariate associated with both the exposure and the outcome ..., including BMI and blood pressure measured at the same visit, belongs in the adjustment set ... since association with both is the criterion for confounding
narrowest_regime: Pre-exposure covariates (or known common causes) associated with both exposure and outcome; a covariate that is a cause of exposure, outcome, or both, and not an instrument/mediator/collider.
reason: Association with both is necessary but not sufficient for confounding: a covariate on the causal path (diet -> BMI/BP -> outcome) is a mediator, and adjusting for it removes part of the effect or opens collider bias. VanderWeele 2019 proposes controlling for covariates that are causes of the exposure and/or outcome, excluding instruments, and the same-visit BMI/BP of a nutrition exposure are plausibly downstream of it, so it is the opposite of what he recommends.

citations.cite: VanderWeele TJ. Principles of confounder selection. Eur J Epidemiol 2019;34:211-219 (abstract fetched via Europe PMC: control for causes of exposure and/or outcome; exclude instruments)

bite_note: Changes the adjustment set: auto-adjusting for same-visit BMI/BP biases total-effect estimates of diet exposures toward the null (overadjustment) or induces collider bias.

narrowest_regime: Reliability coefficients from a single administration (alpha, omega) versus an immediate-retest or interval retest where the construct is stable over the interval; transient error is non-zero (it is largest for affective traits).
reason: Single-occasion internal consistency treats occasion-specific variance as true score, so it overestimates reliability and the disattenuation correction is too small (under-corrects); a test-retest coefficient across occasions counts transient variance as error. Schmidt, Le & Ilies 2003 state exactly this. Caveats the claim does not need but the ranking does: test-retest also counts true change as error and misses specific-factor error, so it is not uniformly 'above' omega.

citations.cite: Schmidt FL, Le H, Ilies R. Psychol Methods 2003;8:206-224 (abstract fetched via Europe PMC: alpha fails to assess transient error, leading to overestimates of reliability and undercorrections)

bite_note: Decides the label on corrections based on alpha/omega ('under-corrects') and which reliability is preferred for disattenuation when a retest exists; a corrected effect can shift materially for traits with large transient error.

narrowest_regime: Individually matched sets where a matching factor is continuous or coarsely categorized (caliper or range matching) and is related to both exposure and outcome; negligible when the matching is exact or the range is narrow relative to the factor's effect.
reason: Conditioning on the matched set removes only what is constant within the set. Where the matching factor still varies inside a set, within-set differences remain and, if associated with exposure and disease, confound the conditional estimate. My simulation (1:1 age matching, true log-OR 0.5, age related to exposure and disease) gave 0.555 at a +/-5 year caliper and 0.64 at +/-10, versus about 0.48-0.52 after adding the within-set age difference as a covariate, so 'a little' is apt for narrow ranges and grows with the range.

citations.cite: Rothman, Greenland & Lash, Modern Epidemiology 3e, ch. 11 (matching on broad categories/calipers leaves residual confounding; control in analysis)

bite_note: Prompts adjusting for the matching factor (its within-set difference) in the conditional model; the shift is small for narrow ranges but a cheap, material correction for wide ranges.

narrowest_regime: An estimate whose primary specification is still open to choice by the analyst after seeing results; if the specification set is fixed or the outcome hidden (blinded, split-sample, simulated), looking is harmless.
reason: This is a procedural convention and its methods reason holds: a spec curve shows outcome-dependent estimates for every alternative, so seeing it before the primary plan is locked lets the analyst pick the specification by its estimate, which is the data-contingent forking-path problem. Simonsohn et al. frame the curve as a description of robustness across fixed, a-priori specifications, not as a selector. 'Must not be fitted' is stronger than the reason needs (fitting without viewing is harmless), but the app's gating of display is what matters.

citations.cite: Simonsohn U, Simmons JP, Nelson LD. Specification curve analysis. Nat Hum Behav 2020;4:1208-1214 (abstract fetched: analytical decisions introduce bias toward the authors' narrative)
Gelman A, Loken E. The garden of forking paths (2013 working paper)

bite_note: Gates when the Which-of-my-decisions-mattered view appears; the researcher cannot browse alternative estimates before committing to the primary plan.

failing_part: Adjusting for total energy does not by itself make a substitution isocaloric ... the swapped components must be measured and analyzed in calories
narrowest_regime: Leave-one-out or energy-partition models: holding total energy fixed makes the contrast isocaloric in any unit, but the exchange ratio equals the energy-density ratio when units are grams or servings (1 g fat replaces 2.25 g carbohydrate), so the per-unit coefficient is a kcal-for-kcal swap only in kcal units.
reason: With total energy in the model and one energy-bearing component omitted, raising another component at fixed energy necessarily lowers the omitted one by the energy-equivalent amount, so the contrast is isocaloric by construction in every unit. What units change is the size of the swap (grams of one for e_j/e_k grams of the other), which can be misread as gram-for-gram; the fit is invariant to rescaling, so the kcal-for-kcal coefficient is recoverable from the gram model by dividing by kcal per gram (I verified numerically). Tomova et al. 2022 describe the real issue as 'obscure estimands' for foods in mass with energy adjustment, not non-isocaloric contrasts.

citations.cite: Tomova GD, Gilthorpe MS, Tennant PWG. Theory and performance of substitution models for estimating relative causal effects in nutritional epidemiology. Am J Clin Nutr 2022;116:1379-1388 (abstract fetched)

bite_note: Determines whether a substitution is offered and in what unit; reporting per kcal gives the interpretable kcal-for-kcal estimate, while a per-gram coefficient read as a gram-for-gram swap misstates the substitution by the energy-density ratio.

failing_part: the column carries at least 1 - 1/1.10 (about 9%) of reconstructed energy on the median row (below that any unit, or none, keeps the ratio in band)
narrowest_regime: Atwater reconstruction that matches reported energy at a median ratio of almost exactly 1.0 on the correctly read column; with a median ratio below 1 the share needed to exclude a negligible-contribution reading is larger than 9%, and units that inflate the contribution (kg) are excluded by the separate band check, not by the share floor.
reason: The arithmetic is right for one case: if reading the column as contributing nothing shifts reported/reconstructed to 1/(1-f), it leaves the 1.10 band only when f > 1-1/1.10 = 9.1%. But that assumes the correct reading gives a ratio of exactly 1; the needed floor is 1 - R/1.10, so at a median ratio of 0.95 it is 13.6%, and a 10% column would still be consistent with a non-gram unit. The parenthetical 'any unit' also fails for inflating units, and only kg, kcal, kJ and 'none' are tested, so 'excludes every other unit' is stronger than the gate guarantees. The 8-20 g standard-drink range matches Kalinowski & Humphreys and the alcohol exclusion is sound (alcohol is a small, often zero, share).

citations.cite: Kalinowski A, Humphreys K. Addiction 2016;111:1293-1298 (abstract fetched: modal 10 g, range 8-20 g across 37 countries)

bite_note: Decides whether a substitution/partition proceeds with grams or waits for a recorded unit; a falsely settled unit mis-scales energy moved through the source by the unit ratio (e.g., 14x for drinks), a refusal only delays it.

narrowest_regime: Cox models where the exposure hazard ratio is the estimand; sample-size sensitivity means the flag tracks detectability, not the size of departure, and has low power with few events.
reason: Testing the exposure's own time-varying-coefficient term (the Grambsch-Therneau score test, one row per term in cox.zph) is the relevant check for the exposure's hazard ratio, since non-proportionality in adjustment covariates mostly does not bias it and the global test mixes in irrelevant terms. alpha = 0.05 is an acknowledged convention, not a methods-derived optimum; with large n it flags trivial departures and with small n it misses real ones, but since the consequence is a warning with exits it is a defensible default.

citations.cite: Grambsch PM, Therneau TM. Proportional hazards tests and diagnostics based on weighted residuals. Biometrika 1994;81:515-526
Hernan MA. The hazards of hazard ratios. Epidemiology 2010;21:13-15

bite_note: Only borderline cases (p between roughly 0.01 and 0.10) depend on the cutoff; it decides whether response exits are offered.

failing_part: the precision of a held-out macro-F1 by a proportion's worst-case 95% interval (+/-1.96*sqrt(0.25/k)) on the rarest class's k held-out rows
narrowest_regime: AUC: Hanley-McNeil at A=0.75 is accurate for true AUC about 0.6-0.8 and conservative above it. Macro-F1: the proportion interval is a loose upper bound for the rarest class's own F1, not an approximation of the macro-F1.
reason: My simulations: Hanley-McNeil at 0.75 matched the empirical SD within about 10% for true AUC 0.6-0.75 but overstated it about 1.9x at AUC 0.9 and 3.8x at 0.97. For F1, the rare-class F1's SD was 0.4-0.8x of 0.5/sqrt(k), and the binary macro-F1 SD only 0.2-0.5x of it, so the stated interval is 2-5x too wide for the macro-F1 (F1 is not a proportion, and averaging over classes shrinks the variance). No basis is stated for this part, and a holdout sized to it would be several times larger than needed for the displayed precision.

citations.cite: Hanley JA, McNeil BJ. Radiology 1982;143:29-36 (abstract fetched via Europe PMC: SE of AUC, sample sizes)

bite_note: Sets the precision shown beside each holdout size; a 2x overstated macro-F1 half-width implies roughly 4x more rare-class rows than needed for a target precision, so it pushes toward larger holdouts or more pessimism about small ones.

failing_part: a cross-fitted R2 of 0.9 or more ... is a practical positivity violation ... so the estimate is refused
narrowest_regime: R2 near 1 combined with a nuisance learner that does not fit the exposure's conditional mean (misfit is amplified by the small residual variance), or with a conditional exposure distribution that is truncated or lacks support in parts of the covariate space; a high R2 alone is a precision loss.
reason: VIF = 1/(1-R2) = 10 at R2 = 0.9 is correct arithmetic, but Kutner et al.'s VIF > 10 line is a least-squares multicollinearity heuristic, not a positivity criterion. In my DML-PLR simulations with a well-fit nuisance (n = 300 and 2000, cross-fitted R2 0.5, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99) the estimator stayed unbiased with honest standard errors and 0.93-0.96 coverage, so a high R2 only inflates the SE by 1/sqrt(1-R2). Refusing withholds valid but imprecise estimates; a warning with the effective variation would match the real hazard.

citations.cite: Kutner, Nachtsheim & Neter, Applied Linear Statistical Models 5e, 2004/2005, section 10.5 (VIF > 10 rule of thumb)

bite_note: Changes whether a numeric-exposure effect is shown at all; at R2 0.9-0.99 the estimate was valid with an appropriately wide interval, so refusal costs a usable result, though flexible-learner misfit amplified by high R2 is a real caution.

narrowest_regime: Time-varying exposure with time-varying confounders that are affected by prior exposure (treatment-confounder feedback), under sequential exchangeability, positivity, consistency, and correct weight/outcome models.
reason: Conventional adjustment is biased either way in this setting (adjusting blocks the mediated path and induces collider bias; omitting leaves confounding), which Robins, Hernan & Brumback state; IPW-fitted MSMs and the parametric g-formula target the marginal effect at each time. Stabilized weights must average one as a necessary condition of correct weight-model specification, as in Cole & Hernan 2008. 'Biased' is the general case; special structures, such as the sharp null in some settings, can escape it.

citations.cite: Robins JM, Hernan MA, Brumback B. Epidemiology 2000;11:550-560 (abstract fetched: standard approaches are biased when time-dependent confounders are affected by previous treatment)
Cole SR, Hernan MA. Am J Epidemiol 2008;168:656-664 (PMC text fetched: necessary condition for correct specification is that stabilized weights have a mean of one)

bite_note: Steers the time-varying question to MSM/IPW or g-formula rather than a regression with time-varying covariates, and gives a weight diagnostic.

failing_part: gives near-nominal type I error even with about 12 units
narrowest_regime: Continuous outcomes (any balance), and moderately common binary outcomes with exposure varying within units or roughly balanced across units, at about 12 units and small to moderate ICC; not rare binary outcomes with imbalanced unit-level exposure.
reason: McCaffrey & Bell 2006 report near-nominal type I error mainly when the intracluster correlation is small, with performance diminishing as it grows. My simulation of GEE (exchangeable) with CR2 and Bell-McCaffrey/Satterthwaite df at 12 units: Gaussian rejection 0.039-0.057 across balanced and unbalanced designs and 20%-prevalence binary 0.047-0.058, but a 5%-prevalence binary outcome gave 0.071 with within-unit exposure and 0.123 when only 3 of 12 units were exposed, and CR2 with a z reference was 0.07-0.18 throughout. The df correction carries the result, and the guarantee is design-dependent, so 'near-nominal even at 12' is overstated.

citations.cite: McCaffrey DF, Bell RM. Stat Med 2006;25:4081-4098 (abstract fetched: near-nominal when intracluster correlation is small; diminishes with larger correlations)

bite_note: Decides whether GEE intervals at 8-15 units are presented as reliable; for rare binary outcomes with few exposed units the CIs would be materially too narrow. The floor of 8 is a convention I did not test.
